chantedPrayers.text:
LIBERATING PRAYER

O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha,
Precious treasury of compassion,
Bestower of supreme inner peace,
You, who love all beings without exception,
Are the source of happiness and goodness;
And you guide us to the liberating path.

Your body is a wishfulfilling jewel,
Your speech is supreme, purifying nectar,
And your mind is refuge for all living beings.

With folded hands I turn to you,
Supreme unchanging friend,
I request from the depths of my heart:

Please give me the light of your wisdom
To dispel the darkness of my mind
And to heal my mental continuum.

Please nourish me with your goodness,
That I in turn may nourish all beings
With an unceasing banquet of delight.

Through your compassionate intention,
Your blessings and virtuous deeds,
And my strong wish to rely upon you,
May all suffering quickly cease
And all happiness and joy be fulfilled;
And may holy Dharma flourish for evermore.

GOING FOR REFUGE

I and all sentient beings, until we achieve enlightenment,
Go for refuge to Buddha, Dharma and Sangha. (3x)

GENERATING BODHICHITTA

Through the virtues I collect by giving and other perfections,
May I become a Buddha for the benefit of all. (3x)

GENERATING THE FOUR IMMEASURABLES

May everyone be happy,
May everyone be free from misery,
May no one ever be separated from their happiness,
May everyone have equanimity, free from hatred and attachment.

VISUALIZING THE FIELD FOR ACCUMULATING MERIT

In the space before me is the living Buddha Shakyamuni surrounded by all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, like the full moon surrounded by stars.

PRAYER OF SEVEN LIMBS

With my body, speech and mind, humbly I prostrate,
And make offerings both set out and imagined.
I confess my wrong deeds from all time,
And rejoice in the virtues of all.
Please stay until samsara ceases,
And turn the Wheel of Dharma for us.
I dedicate all virtues to great enlightenment.

OFFERING THE MANDALA

The ground sprinkled with perfume and spread with flowers,
The Great Mountain, four lands, sun and moon,
Seen as a Buddha Land and offered thus,
May all beings enjoy such Pure Lands.

I offer without any sense of loss
The objects that give rise to my attachment, hatred and confusion,
My friends, enemies and strangers, our bodies and enjoyments;
Please accept these and bless me to be released directly from the three poisons.

IDAM GURU RATNA MANDALAKAM NIRYATAYAMI

PRAYER OF THE STAGES OF THE PATH

The path begins with strong reliance
On my kind Teacher, source of all good;
O Bless me with this understanding
To follow him with great devotion.

This human life with all its freedoms,
Extremely rare, with so much meaning;
O Bless me with this understanding
All day and night to seize its essence.

My body, like a water bubble,
Decays and dies so very quickly;
After death come results of karma,
Just like the shadow of a body.

With this firm knowledge and remembrance
Bless me to be extremely cautious,
Always avoiding harmful actions
And gathering abundant virtue.

Samsara's pleasures are deceptive,
Give no contentment, only torment;
So please bless me to strive sincerely
To gain the bliss of perfect freedom.

O Bless me so that from this pure thought
Come mindfulness and greatest caution,
To keep as my essential practice
The doctrine's root, the Pratimoksha.

Just like myself all my kind mothers
Are drowning in samsara's ocean;
O So that I may soon release them,
Bless me to train in bodhichitta.

But I cannot become a Buddha
By this alone without three ethics;
So bless me with the strength to practice
The Bodhisattva's ordination.

By pacifying my distractions
And analyzing perfect meanings,
Bless me to quickly gain the union
Of special insight and quiescence.

When I become a pure container
Through common paths, bless me to enter
The essence practice of good fortune,
The supreme vehicle, Vajrayana.

The two attainments both depend on
My sacred vows and my commitments;
Bless me to understand this clearly
And keep them at the cost of my life.

By constant practice in four sessions,
The way explained by holy Teachers,
O Bless me to gain both the stages,
Which are the essence of the Tantras.

May those who guide me on the good path,
And my companions all have long lives;
Bless me to pacify completely
All obstacles, outer and inner.

May I always find perfect Teachers,
And take delight in holy Dharma,
Accomplish all grounds and paths swiftly,
And gain the state of Vajradhara.

RECEIVING BLESSINGS AND PURIFYING

From the hearts of all the holy beings, streams of light and nectar flow down, granting blessings and purifying.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text: Meditation on bodhisattva vows. The purpose of this meditation is to strengthen our intention to take and keep the bodhisattva's vows and to live the bodhisattva's way of life. We can consider: when we have prepared and developed our mind sufficiently to be able to practice the six perfections leading to enlightenment, we're ready to take the actual bodhisattva vows. The purpose of taking these vows is to accomplish the aim of a bodhisattva. What is this aim? To attain enlightenment for the benefit of all mother sentient beings. It is not sufficient just to wish to attain Buddhahood for the benefit of others. We must take the proper vows and engage in all the necessary practices.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text: Again, when we have prepared and developed our mind sufficiently to be able to practice the six perfections leading to enlightenment, we're ready to take the actual bodhisattva vows. The purpose of taking these vows is to accomplish the aim of a bodhisattva. What is this aim? To attain enlightenment for the benefit of all mother sentient beings. It is not sufficient just to wish to attain Buddhahood for the benefit of others. We must take the proper vows and engage in all the necessary practices. Spend time really considering these points and especially why it is necessary to take the vows to practice the six perfections in order to attain enlightenment.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text: Through reflecting on the importance of taking the bodhisattva vows, an intention arises, thinking: to attain enlightenment, I need to take and keep the bodhisattva vows. Then we can hold this intention single-pointedly for as long as possible. If we become distracted, we can return back to considering the importance of taking the bodhisattva vows to attain enlightenment.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text: Then again, when a strong determination to take and keep these vows arises, we can do placement meditation, concentrating on this determination. Just really hold this determination. I want to take and keep the bodhisattva vows because there is no enlightenment outside of this.

guidedMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
guidedMeditation.text: Just keep this determination in our heart for the final minute, and in our own time, we can gradually arise from our practice.

postMeditation.speaker: Kadam Kyle
postMeditation.text: Welcome back everyone. Happy rainy day. We even have a little metronome beat going on in our air conditioning system, some kind of leak in there, so it's very exciting here. So then, let's see. We need a reader from verse 26 through 34. Yes, thank you. Can someone pass her the mic?

shantidevaReading.text:
(26) Now my life has borne great fruit,
My human life has attained great meaning;
Today I am born into the lineage of Buddha
And have become a Bodhisattva.

(27) All my actions from now on
Shall accord with this noble lineage;
And upon this lineage, pure and faultless,
I shall never bring disgrace.

(28) Just as it is rare indeed
For a blind person to find a jewel in a heap of rubbish,
So too, by some very rare chance,
I have generated bodhichitta.

(29) It is the supreme nectar that overcomes
The dominion of death over living beings,
And an inexhaustible treasury
That dispels all their poverty.

(30) It is the supreme medicine that relieves
The sickness of living beings,
And a shady tree that provides shelter
For weary beings travelling samsara's paths.

(31) It is a universal bridge by which all living beings
Can be delivered from the lower realms,
And a rising moon of a mind
That relieves the torment of their delusions.

(32) It is a vast sun that completely dispels
The fog of unknowing from living beings.
It is the quintessential butter that arises
When the milk of Dharma is churned.

(33) For the honoured guests, the beings on samsara's paths
Who wish to enjoy the delights of bliss,
Bodhichitta will satisfy them all
By leading them to the supreme state of bliss.

(34) Today, in the presence of all the Protectors,
I invite all living beings to be my guests
To enjoy these temporary and ultimate delights.
May gods, demi-gods and everyone else be joyful!

practiceReports.speaker: David
practiceReports.text: I enjoyed reviewing the 46 secondary downfalls and 18 root downfalls. Nice trip down memory lane from when we studied the bodhisattva vow. And I appreciated what you said about finding any vows that don't seem quite right and that that's the difference between me and a bodhisattva. One that jumped out was indulging in frivolity — singing and dancing and so forth. I was like, oh, this is kind of a bummer. I sort of get it intellectually — you're not making every moment count if you do that. But anyway, I was like, all right, well, I got a little ways to go before I'm a real bodhisattva. But then some of the other ones were so practical and helpful. The ones that jumped out were making no effort to control our anger — basically, if you get angry and then you just kind of let that moment pass without doing anything about it, then that's essentially a secondary downfall. And I found that helpful to recognize that actually something needs to happen after you get angry. There should be some kind of response inwardly. And if there's not, then that's what the downfall was pointing to. Or neglecting to train in mental stabilization — sometimes that seems like a nice-to-have kind of thing, but it's like, no, if you're not training in meditating, then that's also not it. And then the other one was not acting in accordance with the inclinations of others. There was this situation this morning — I've realized that there's times on the weekends where, depending on how the evening goes, there's literally not enough time for me to go to bed at the same time as my wife and then meditate in the morning and then walk the dog together. The math doesn't work for that equation. And today I was just like, all right, I'm going to postpone my practice, we'll take the dog out together, and then practice afterwards. And I felt like that was the right move. I could tell that she was very happy with that. I used to be so attached to like, no, practice is most important, but actually it's not. It was a little bit of a downfall with regards to that vow, I felt. So that was a nice little insight I got from thinking about that.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, thanks, David. It's lovely. Just revisiting the different secondary and root downfalls and trying to see the practical application and inferring that each one is a practice. It's not an idea. It's not words. It's a practice, something that we do actively, just like every piece of Dharma. So yeah, it's nice that you could kind of mine them and explore them. Sumit, yeah.

practiceReports.text: You're almost definitely right because it was all messed up and I just set what I could.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Oh, okay. Yeah. It would be nice to not have to project. It would be nice just to be comfortable and talk normal. So it does usually — yeah, I think that's really nice for me. That's a nice volume. Is that okay? Everyone's all right? Okay. Thanks, Sumit. Yeah, on to you.

practiceReports.speaker: Sumit
practiceReports.text: All right, two things. First of all, I guess I was closer to being a bodhisattva than I knew because I'm a terrible singer and dancer and therefore I hate singing and dancing. So basically, there. The second thing was about — so I had really gotten into this vow thing and I sat with that a lot, really taking a vow from my heart. Not just touching it with your mouth — I've done that a million times. And I thought about when I really did take the bodhisattva vow, or a version of that, with my heart. There was this person who I really loved and she was suffering a lot, and I really wanted to help her. And it was very clear to me that me in this limited state could not do so. And in a very heartfelt way I took this vow: I'm going to work to become a Buddha so I can help you. I didn't say those Buddhist words to her, but I said to her, I will always love you no matter what, forever. And it was a really strong, heartfelt — that was like a bodhisattva vow coming from my heart. It wasn't all living beings, to be fair, but it was like, for this person, I will always work to become a Buddha to help you. And that really came from my heart. And that experience — the overall situation is actually quite tumultuous and hard because basically the person I love is suffering. But in that moment it's so serene. It's like, I'm always going to do this, no matter what. And there's this great serenity and peacefulness in that moment of taking a vow. So I was reflecting on that. Most of the time when I was thinking about taking this vow with my heart, what was coming up for me was very martial, military. If you guys know the show Game of Thrones — the Night's Watch, they take this vow: I'm going to protect the realm. And it's really heartfelt: I'm going to do this. There was definitely a sense of resolve, but the energy was coming out of my personal integrity and personal belief — like, I can do this. That's basically me looking at the storm, being in the middle of a storm. Imagine you're in the middle of a hurricane and you're going to walk across to save someone. The wind's blowing at you and you're like, I'm going to do this. And that's what samsara is — it's really hard. We shouldn't fool ourselves to think this isn't anything but that. But you have to be like, I'm going to do this. But the vow for the person I love — I can believe I'm going to keep loving this person. I can really believe that. It's a stronger fuel. Versus 'I believe I can overcome this' — that's just so much more powerful. That insight really hit me about taking the bodhisattva vow for the benefit of all. That's an important clause. It's not just so that others can benefit, but it's so that I can keep the vow. That's the energy it takes for me to keep this vow — the energy of love versus the energy of my own personal integrity.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, those are great points, Sumit. Thank you. It makes total sense. There's a couple important things there. One is, yeah, the bodhisattva is said to go from joy to joy. So the energy is actually of joy, but the joy is coming, as you noted, from that lack of self-interest, from that love of others. There is an intensity we can call on from a point of view of self-interest, but it's not particularly joyful. It's very intense and it can get jobs done, but it definitely doesn't scale and last for a long time. It breaks down at some point. It's really only our love for all living beings — taking that one person that you're really loving and caring for and trying to help, but then extrapolating that to all living beings — that's the love that will carry us to enlightenment. So it's just really nice that you're bringing out these ideas. That was part of the exercise — to really think about when we've taken the vow in a way that moved our heart and what was going on there. And if that hasn't happened, then it's an invitation to think about how to do that. Thanks, Sumit. Great points. Others please. Suzanne, yeah, and then Adriana after that.

practiceReports.speaker: Suzanne
practiceReports.text: I'm not sure if that was alive and well in my mind. I even noticed it on the way over — I took a car and I was thinking, I was a little nervous because of the weather. And I was doing one of my six Vajrayogini sessions, and as I was dissolving myself, I was saying, no, I don't want to die! I want to go to class! So I knew that wasn't where I was supposed to be. And the other thing I want to report is I've just totally gone off the rails with the phone — the no-phone thing. I was pretty good over the summer. I was good when I was in England. But the more tired I am, the more I want to be on there. And I'm finding I'm going to sleep 45 minutes to an hour later than I would like, and it just throws off everything. And it's so bad, and it's agitating. I know all the things I'm supposed to be doing, I'm just not doing them. I could maybe just take the phone and put it under my mattress. I don't know what else to do with it. So I just wanted to report my struggles.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, thanks, Suzanne. It's helpful to share. Basically, until we uproot the seeds of delusion in our mind, they'll keep coming back over and over again. They're like little loopholes that keep getting exploited. As long as there's a seed of delusion, it will keep coming back. And so that's why we have to realize emptiness and become Vajrayogini or Heruka. But until then, they're going to keep coming back, and we need increasingly sophisticated tools and methods to keep them at bay — to repel them or suppress them. So this is often going to happen. We set up a technique or a strategy, it's going to reduce the delusions for a period of time, but then different environmental factors change or life changes in some way, and then our strategy either becomes inert and doesn't really work, or we forget about it, and then the delusion comes back. Pops right back up — hey, remember me? And it can come very forcefully. Just because we've previously dealt with it doesn't mean it's not latent in all of its majesty — or horror. From one point of view, when these cycles happen, we need to use that as motivation, through purification practice and also through realizing emptiness, because this is annoying. It's annoying when that happens. We put the work in, we move forward, and then it feels like we've been reverted. In reality, we haven't totally reverted — we've learned a lesson and we have seen that change is possible in the past. So we are forward. And in these moments, we have to figure out what changed, what didn't work, what's the lesson here. As you noted — tiredness, okay, seeing if that's a factor. That's a condition to think about. But there might have been other conditions too. It might have just been the resolve went a bit limp, and that happens sometimes too. And that's an invitation: I have to keep re-upping and re-strengthening the resolve itself. So there are these lessons that we learn along the way, which are great. Thanks for sharing, Suzanne. There's definitely a good way forward somewhere. It's definitely worth time and effort to assassinate that distraction Mara, because it's bad news for all of us. Thank you. Adriana, yes.

practiceReports.speaker: Adriana
practiceReports.text: Hi. So two weeks ago I met this woman on the subway — she was living in the subway station. Her name was Grafina. She's Roma, and she had a little baby. She had this sign. And I have this rule: the first person I see, I'm going to really take time to help them. If I see other people, I'm going to flick nectar at them, I'm going to pray for them. But the first person — okay, I want to find out what's going on. So we had a little conversation and I gave her some money. And I was like, I'm just going to sit with you. If I sit with you, maybe more people will give you money. And I kept thinking of her. Then I saw her again, and this week I was practicing. I just kept saying, I have a promise. I made a promise. And just enjoying and feeling more energized by this commitment that I made. And so I saw her again and I was like, Grafina! And she was like, you remembered my name! She was just totally blown away. And I was like, I love you so much. This time instead of one kid she had three kids. It was all worse. But I was like, it's going to be fine. The thing that made me so happy was that before, when I had tried to help her, it felt very intellectual — like, I'm thinking about it, I'm like, yes, I have to add her to my list, I'm going to get enlightened for Grafina. But then when I had this big promise in my heart, I was like, I'm going to make it lighter and just be better at helping people. Because it was less intellectual and more heartfelt. And I could tell — the most important thing maybe was that I remembered her name, not just that I had money to give her. So we have this wisdom that will come more from that intuition of the love.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: And that was what we were trying to get at last class — this idea of 'we promised.' We promised to attain enlightenment for the benefit of all living beings. It's a promise. We made it to the Buddhas. On our karmic stamp, we promised it. We kind of put up our own karma on that, saying, I'm going to do it — on my karmic legacy, I'm going to do this. Which is a huge commitment, actually. It's a very weighty commitment to make, to promise something like that. So you're kind of making the point of calling on this idea: I promised. It's a promise. We start to get this feeling — this is my role in life. My job is to benefit others, help others. It's not to go to work. It's not to make money. It's not to go get a croissant or whatever the sub-games of life we're into. We have one main goal, one main job: to benefit others. And everything else is supporting that. And that just makes everything very comfortable and natural, as you noticed. It's like when people are interrogating someone who they think is lying — they ask them their story, but then they ask a bunch of specific questions, and they can notice they're filling in details with made-up stuff. Because you're calling on something that's phony. But for the person who that story is real, they can just fill in any amount of detail. 'So why did you do that?' 'Oh, because of this.' 'What did you do next?' 'Oh, I did that.' It's all just organic and natural, because that's just who we are. For the bodhisattva, if we really are holding that view — my job is to benefit others — then when situations come up, it's just natural. We're not trying to do some internal calculation of what to do, what to say, how to be. I'm just going to be who I am. That's my job — to benefit others. So as you noted, we say their name — of course. But if it's a very calculated 'I'm going to be a good person now because I'm supposed to,' then it's all just — versus just, my job is to benefit others. That's who I am. Okay, now I'm naturally just going to do that. Actually, there's a better example. A really good actor is like this. If they're really into the part, then if someone goes off script, they respond based on how the character would respond. If you're really into being Lady Macbeth or something like that, and someone you're acting with accidentally says the wrong line or does the wrong thing, you just act like Lady Macbeth would act — you just cut their throat, or whatever she would do — immediately. But if you're not into the part and someone goes off script, you get very confused. Because all you know is this very stunted, mechanistic version — 'when they say this, then I say that.' You're not embodying the character. In the same way, when we're embodying the bodhisattva role — we're embodying it. I made this promise. Situations come up in life and we're just naturally able to flow with it and respond as the bodhisattva would. Anyway, thanks so much, Adriana. Mimi, yes.

practiceReports.speaker: Mimi
practiceReports.text: Hi. So I also reviewed the bodhisattva vows this week and tried to see which one jumped out at me. The one that came up was not acting in ways that cause others to generate faith — like being a good example through my actions. So this is what happened. Recently I've had to move into a different office. I had a very nice office with a huge desk, and now I've had to move into this very busy area that I share with a whole bunch of doctors and residents and students. They're constantly coming and going. And there's a new group of residents that have arrived, and I noticed that I had made a judgment about one of the young doctors. I had put her into this category of 'really annoying know-it-all privileged person.' And I thought to myself, that's not very nice, Mimi. And I kind of just shot her off — not really paying much attention to her. And so on Friday, she was on call, and I could see that she was really tired and really anxious. And I had been listening to a podcast of Ken Rapton, who was talking about doing things from a place of love — about your intention and thinking about what do you want for that person, how can you benefit them. And I thought — it was right at 5 PM, and everybody was getting ready to leave, and she got an emergency consult. And I could see her sighing and getting really tight in her space. So I decided, I just walked over to her and said, hey, don't worry. You've got this. You know what to do. Before you know it, you'll be off being on call, and all this will be gone. And she stood up and she just hugged me. She said, oh man, I really needed that. Thank you so much. So it just reminded me how quickly we can make judgments about other people. We don't know what they're going through. And that kindness is so easy. Ken Rapton said in his podcast, put the sugar in first. And when you come from love, then everything is easier and sweeter. So that's how I practiced this week.

practiceReports.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceReports.text: Yeah, thanks, Mimi. That's great. It makes total sense. You're revisiting the bodhisattva vows and especially setting a good example — acting in ways that help people generate faith. And just thinking about love. This is a great example. We put someone in a box, maybe with a judgmental mind, have some story about them. Then we remember — I'm a bodhisattva. I'm not someone who puts people in boxes and rigidly stays with them. My job is to benefit people. How can I help this person who I previously misjudged? And then our mind just becomes flexible, and we're able to make a difference. And we're just so much happier, honestly. It's a really nice example — especially about assuming things about other people where we have no idea what's going on in them. Bringing the bodhisattva's way of life is always the right approach. Thank you.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: Okay, good. So then, let's see where to begin. So we're at concluding activities, I believe page 136. Geshe says here: 'So far Shantideva has described the various preparatory practices useful for accumulating merit and the ceremony involved in fully accepting bodhichitta. The activities that seal and conclude our full acceptance of the mind of enlightenment can be explained in three sections as follows: meditating on the happiness of fulfilling our own wishes, meditating on the happiness of benefiting others and fulfilling their wishes, and exhorting others to meditate on happiness.' There's three happinesses and three meditates in these three. So I wonder — if we check in with ourselves, it would be nice to ask: how is my meditation going? We're talking seated here — seated meditation. How's it going? And do I feel very confident that I'm meditating according to the Kadampa tradition of meditation? Using preparatory practices, then using analytical meditation to find the object of meditation, and then doing placement meditation on the object of meditation. And then we get distracted, come back to the analytical meditation, get the object of meditation again, practice placement meditation on that object. So we can just check: is our actual meditation practice like that? Is that what's going on? Are those the steps that go on? And if we teach meditation — like some of us teach classes, because we're a meditation center — when we're guiding meditations, are they in accordance with that structure? Are we giving people the analytical meditation, the object, and the placement meditation?

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: Even more precisely, in the Mirror of Dharma with Additions, the way the Lamrim meditations are structured is sort of the best presentation. Geshe even said this — it's the best presentation of how to meditate. And with those, there's the purpose, the object, and the actual meditation. So at the end of class today and going forward, we're going to try to extract the meditation break practice. But I'd also like us to identify what's the actual meditation we're going to be doing in class. And when we do that, I'm going to request whoever says something to give these three things. What's the purpose — basically why are we doing this? What's the object — so what's the specific insight that this meditation is leading to? And then what's the actual meditation — which is sort of like, what do you think about to get to the object?

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: For example, in the meditation we just did: the purpose is so that we attain enlightenment through basically taking and keeping the bodhisattva vows. That was the purpose of that meditation. The object of meditation was a strong determination to take and keep the bodhisattva vows. The actual meditation was considering the benefits and the good things that we get from taking and keeping the bodhisattva vows, and why that is necessary to attain enlightenment. So that's the structure. The purpose gives us the buy-in — that's the 'why.' It's the benefits of something. It gives us wishing faith and admiring faith in what we're actually doing. Clarifying the object so that people actually know where they're going. And the actual meditation — okay, now we're going to go there. I think even in the little meditation app that's around, if you listen, you'll be able to track these parts. There's like 15 or 20 meditations — I don't know how many exactly — but I think if you listen, you'll be able to see the facets of these three in there, if you need examples. Outside just the Lamrim meditations — the Lamrim meditations are very clearly designed — the idea that we're trying to work towards is, how do you extract the structure? For example, in the section we're about to look at. As we go through here, we should be thinking, okay, what's the meditation here? How do I craft a meditation out of this? What's the purpose? What's the object? What's the actual meditation? In reality, that's how we should always be thinking, because that's the way a practitioner thinks — how am I going to take these Dharma teachings and turn them into an experience in my life? And as a teacher, obviously we need to do that. But as a practitioner, at the very least, we need to do that ourselves. So I just wanted to note that. I'm very curious to see what we come up with. Maybe when we get to the discussion at the end of class, do that first before doing anything else. And then when you reach a conclusion with your partner — okay, we've got the purpose, object, actual meditation — then do anything else. Is that okay? Anyone have any questions specifically about that point? David, yes.

mainTeaching.speaker: David
mainTeaching.text: It's about the purpose. I found when I was going through the Mirror of Dharma — we had the meditation calendar group — the purpose was very surprising. It would always lead to the next meditation. The purpose of compassion was to develop bodhichitta. And the purpose of bodhichitta is to become enlightened. Even though the thing you're actually meditating on is kind of a step before that. So I don't know if that's common to all of them, but the purpose of everything is to benefit all living beings, eliminate suffering, and become happy. Anyway, I don't know if there's any pointers you could share about how to scope the purpose.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: Yeah, good question. In the Mirror of Dharma sections, some of the purposes are directly linked to inducing the next meditation experience. So great compassion is a very clear example of that. Not all of them are like that — for example, the death meditation, the purpose is to help us overcome laziness of attachment. But yeah, some of them are explicitly linked to the next one. So part of that is because that's one of the reasons the Lamrim meditations are in the order that they're in — because why do we actually meditate on great compassion? To develop bodhichitta. Without great compassion, you can't ever get bodhichitta. Without bodhichitta, you can never practice the six perfections. Without practicing the six perfections, you can't become enlightened. So actually, that purpose is incredibly important. Thinking, wow, it's with great compassion that I'll be able to develop bodhichitta, which will eventually be why I can attain enlightenment. That purpose is very important. But it's not the only aspect of the purpose. The whole section is the purpose. It's not just that first line. The first line is like the main selling point, and then everything else is additional selling points that build up the case. Some of it is background knowledge, but it's basically helping us get to a greater purpose. And you need the background knowledge to get to that purpose. So for our sake and for the point of view of guiding ourselves and others in meditation, we can think: the purpose is basically the 'why.' Why is this a meditation? Why are we doing this? That's a very simple way to do it. We can include the background information that establishes the 'why,' or we can just keep it simple — these are the benefits, these are the things you get from it, this is what will happen from it. Even if it's breathing meditation — what's the purpose? Anyone want to throw out what's the purpose of breathing meditation?

mainTeaching.speaker: Sumit
mainTeaching.text: Is it to still your mind so that you can focus your mind on a meditation object?

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: Yeah, I think that's a nice one. You can also just do something like 'to quiet distraction so that we could experience some peace of mind.' When breathing meditation is a preliminary, it's definitely what you're describing. If it was just in a class as the sole meditation, it would be more like overcoming distractions so that we could experience some peace. Any of those are great. But when you're guiding the meditation, it's actually nice to say, 'this is the purpose' — even just one line: 'the purpose of this meditation is...' And then, okay, now we get into guiding the meditation. Any other questions about this point? Okay, thank you.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: So that's meditation. Then the text: 'Meditating on the happiness of fulfilling our own wishes. Once we have developed the precious bodhichitta, we will realize the great extent of our good fortune and rejoice accordingly. In order to enhance all the qualities associated with bodhichitta, we should be full of praise and encouragement, uplifting ourselves with joy.' 'Now my life has borne great fruit, my human life has attained great meaning.' We should think how privileged we are to take the bodhisattva vows, and how this action has given great meaning to our human rebirth, making it truly fruitful. Thinking in this way, we will be filled with profound happiness. Having studied Mahayana Dharma and meditated on and developed bodhichitta, we have discovered qualities of life that are not ordinarily possessed. This very precious mind of bodhichitta is not easily found in this world. Scholars may study hard and obtain doctorates and other advanced degrees — these qualifications cannot begin to compare with the precious mind of bodhichitta. Therefore, the person who has developed this precious mind has great reason to rejoice and be happy. We should think: 'Today I am born into the lineage of Buddha and have become a bodhisattva. All my actions from now on shall accord with this noble lineage, and upon this lineage, pure and faultless, I shall never bring disgrace.'

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: So that verse — verse 26 and 27 — these are really famous verses that you actually explicitly recite in various bodhisattva vow ceremonies. And it's really nice to learn these words. You'll find they're very melodic and beautiful and easy to learn. They just flow very naturally. They're lovely to recite in the day. In the morning, you can retake your bodhisattva vows and think: 'Now my life has borne great fruit, my human life has attained great meaning. Today I am born into the lineage of Buddha and have become a bodhisattva. All my actions from now on shall accord with this noble lineage, and upon this lineage, pure and faultless, I shall never bring disgrace.' It's like we got knighted a bodhisattva. I'm part of something very noble and special, and I'm going to do it right. I'm going to really respect this privilege that I've been given in this life. I've been initiated into a very noble cause. We can learn these words and recite them and try to connect to the feeling here. Part of this is that this feeling of happiness when we take a vow is actually part of taking the vow. I'm not sure if we're all aware of that — the feeling of happiness that we have that vow, a little blissful happy feeling — that's really like we've now taken the vow. So it's a crucial part of taking the bodhisattva vow. That's why it's included in the various vow ceremonies, where we say, 'Okay, now be happy that you've taken the vow.' And that happiness, feeling that happiness, is kind of like locking it in.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: 'Then it is very rare to find a precious jewel in a heap of rubbish, and rarer still for a blind man to discover such a jewel. If a blind man were to be so fortunate, how happy he would become. In a similar fashion, it is very rare to find a person who is even interested in trying to develop bodhichitta, and rarer still to find someone who has actually developed it. If we were to develop such a precious mind, how happy and joyful we would be. There is no quality in life greater than having developed the engaging mind of bodhichitta. A great teacher of the past was once asked: what is better — developing miracle powers and clairvoyance, receiving visions of our personal deity, or developing bodhichitta? He answered that bodhichitta is a thousand times greater than any other accomplishment or power. Why? In many previous lives, we have developed miracle powers and have even been able to fly in the sky. During the first aeon of this world age, all beings possessed clairvoyance and had bodies of the nature of light. But where is the essence of these powers now? What benefit have they brought any of us? Everything is changing and we are still caught up in the round of samsara, experiencing suffering and dissatisfaction continuously. However, if we had previously developed the thought of bodhichitta and engaged in its practices, by now we might have gained the enlightenment of Buddhahood and be free from the problems of samsara.'

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: So the point here is that developing bodhichitta has this kind of deterministic relationship with enlightenment. That's the point being raised. There's lots of other qualities you can develop that don't guarantee that we attain enlightenment. You can invest lots of time and lifetimes even developing other qualities, but have nothing to show for it. That's what Geshe is trying to talk about here. We kind of put our chips in lots of different baskets and actually attain certain spiritual insights and realizations in past lives, but none of them have the same guaranteed inevitability — the deterministic relationship with enlightenment — that bodhichitta has. It definitely leads to attaining enlightenment. So we want to have this feeling like it's the best strategic investment in our time, the best quality that guarantees to pay out in the long run. Nothing else fits the bill in the same way. Part of this is reflecting on this feeling: 'Upon this lineage, pure and faultless, I'll never bring disgrace.' Feeling joyful and happy taking these bodhisattva vows. It's like, okay, now I'm really focusing on the one checkpoint that's going to guarantee I move to enlightenment. This will definitely lead there. And we just feel like we're on the exact right path. You can even think about all our past lives where we've had spiritual inclinations and imprints. We've trained our mind, gained even miracle powers from tranquil abiding and incredible concentration. We went really far down these different spiritual paths in many lives and really worked our butt off. But we went down a path that doesn't have its result as enlightenment — it has its result usually in some kind of form realm or formless realm god rebirth, which is incredibly blissful and mind-blowing, but it's not enlightenment. So eventually you do come back down. Finally, we found the door out to full enlightenment. All those past selves in our continuum — their hard work is finally vindicated and free of that search.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: 'Developing bodhichitta is even more important than receiving visions of our personal deity and engaging in related tantric practices. By meditating on our channels, winds, and drops, we can develop inner heat and even be able to levitate into space. However, without bodhichitta, all this is meaningless. If we've developed bodhichitta and gained an understanding of emptiness, such tantric practices can be very useful in increasing our realizations. But if we lack this foundation, we'll be completely unable to practice the tantric path. Many people nowadays are attracted to tantra because they believe it will provide a shortcut to enlightenment or at least endow them with magical powers. But these people have no understanding of how important the foundation of renunciation, bodhichitta, and emptiness is for this higher path. Practicing tantra solely for the sake of benefiting this life, hoping to gain renown or special powers, does nothing but plant the seeds for hellish suffering in the future. Anyone who practices like this is like a misguided person who uses precious sandalwood to kindle a fire. Or, to cite other examples, such an ill-motived practitioner is like a person who uses banknotes to light a cigarette, or a Rolls-Royce to cart manure. If we wish to make the practice of tantra meaningful, bodhichitta is indispensable.'

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: So here Geshe is really getting at the Lamrim and the structure of realizations that we need to go to progressively higher and higher states and eventually attain enlightenment. It's like a stack — there's an order, and you need a certain foundation. On that foundation you can build another level, and on that level another level. If you don't get the order right, enlightenment's not possible. We might be able to do something, but it's not enlightenment. Let's say we were all in a race to build a structure that's as high as a 50-story building. You could do some things that will get you far ahead in the lead — like get a bunch of metal poles and have them be really tall. At first it would look like, wow, I'm ahead, I've got 10 stories of a metal pole popping up into the sky. But at some point, you're not going to get to 50 stories. It's going to topple over from its own weight. There's not going to be a firm foundation to hold that thing in the ground. So all that work to get your really cool 10-story pole is actually a total waste — it has nothing to do with a 50-story building. It looks like it's getting ahead, but it's actually a diversion. What you need is a crazy huge foundation. That's what you really need. If you see some of these building projects going around here, you'll see they're just digging deep into the ground. That's what they do first. They dig really deep and you're like, I don't even know why you need to go that deep. It's because they have to lay some really deep foundation.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: This stack of renunciation, bodhichitta, and emptiness — it's only on the layer of bodhichitta that we can gain a perfect realization of emptiness. We can gain one that a Hinayana practitioner can get, but it's not a perfect realization. It's only with bodhichitta that we can get a perfect realization — ultimate bodhichitta, which is actually a Mahayana path, a path of seeing. And it's only with that that we're going to actually attain enlightenment. So this is like this stack, this order. It's tempting to try all these little shortcuts along the way, and that's akin to getting your 10-story pole up. It looks like, 'Look at me, I'm so great!' But actually, digging the big hole is the closer step. The practice can look like we're taking shortcuts and skipping steps, but at some point, they utterly falter and fail. When we understand that, we can really appreciate the Lamrim structure, which has this exact understanding in mind. Each step along the way might look superfluous at first. Why do I have to keep doing meditations on the dangers of lower rebirth over and over? Why do I have to keep doing meditations on death over and over? But at some point, we're going to have this realization: this is an absolute necessity to go further. For example, if we don't do the death meditation, any time we get good spiritual qualities, we're going to get prideful and attached. And then go back down again. It's not until we've actually abandoned our attachment that we humbly, really move forward. Anyway, the point is simple: bodhichitta is an absolutely necessary step for enlightenment. These higher practices only really work on the basis of some kind of similitude of bodhichitta. The Lamrim helps us appreciate this order of practice. Without developing our mind through these meditations, at some point we're going to realize, 'Oh, I missed a key initial step.' And a very sad thing at that point is, you have to just kind of restart and learn that step from the ground up. So it's better to follow the path, especially the Lamrim, which is laid out very beautifully.

mainTeaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
mainTeaching.text: Okay, so that's that section. In the next, we're going to be looking at meditating on the happiness of benefiting others and fulfilling their wishes. And I think we'll be able to get a little further than that. Okay, good. That's it.

dedication.speaker: Kadam Kyle
dedication.text: Let's dedicate here, and we'll come back at 6:10. You can think: through the virtues we've collected through practicing, meditating, discussing — may all living beings find lasting peace of mind, enlightenment. We can make any personal prayers or dedications.

chantedPrayers.text:
LIBERATING PRAYER

O Blessed One, Shakyamuni Buddha,
Precious treasury of compassion,
Bestower of supreme inner peace,
You, who love all beings without exception,
Are the source of happiness and goodness;
And you guide us to the liberating path.

Your body is a wishfulfilling jewel,
Your speech is supreme, purifying nectar,
And your mind is refuge for all living beings.

With folded hands I turn to you,
Supreme unchanging friend,
I request from the depths of my heart:

Please give me the light of your wisdom
To dispel the darkness of my mind
And to heal my mental continuum.

Please nourish me with your goodness,
That I in turn may nourish all beings
With an unceasing banquet of delight.

Through your compassionate intention,
Your blessings and virtuous deeds,
And my strong wish to rely upon you,
May all suffering quickly cease
And all happiness and joy be fulfilled;
And may holy Dharma flourish for evermore.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Remember those? Obviously. Or 'nimkabu.' If you want to go more Bridge than Universal on that last word, to help remember it. First of all, bodhichitta is like supreme nectar that is able to overcome the great power of death. It destroys the suffering of death by leading all sentient beings to the eternal, unsurpassable state of complete Buddhahood. Bodhichitta is also like an inexhaustible treasury that eliminates the poverty of all sentient beings by satisfying all their wishes. How do Buddhas and Bodhisattvas — those supreme beings who possess bodhichitta — eliminate poverty? By providing us with inexhaustible Dharma teachings and material gifts, they can temporarily fulfill our spiritual and physical needs. Furthermore, by leading us to the everlasting state of happiness and complete enlightenment, they can ultimately free us from all poverty. It is in this respect that bodhichitta is like an inexhaustible treasury.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: If bodhichitta has such power, why is it that so many beings in this and other realms are still experiencing poverty and so forth? The reason is that the power of enlightened beings is like an iron hook. And for us to be pulled up from our own suffering, we must make a connection with this hook by our own ring of faith. If we do not turn our mind to the Three Jewels, there is no way for them to help us. The causes for our release are not yet complete. If we remain passive, waiting for our salvation to come from the outside without doing anything from our own side to develop our mind, we will continue to experience suffering as we have always done.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Returning to Shantideva's analogy: bodhichitta is like supreme medicine that can relieve the mental and physical sickness of all sentient beings. Once we have taken the medicine of bodhichitta, we will gradually be cured of all diseases of body and mind. With his or her mind continuously filled with the medicine of bodhichitta, a bodhisattva is immune to suffering. Just as a shady tree provides refreshment for a tired traveler, bodhichitta provides shade and rest for the exhausted sentient beings wandering along the paths of samsara. And finally, bodhichitta is like a universal bridge that leads beings from the suffering of the lower realms to the happiness of the higher realms, and ultimately to Buddhahood.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: So yeah, the point of this little section is like — woohoo, bodhichitta! That's the feeling we're trying to get, which is a faith in bodhichitta. It's admiring faith and then wishing faith: I really want to develop this mind. So we're working on our little delusion issues. We haven't let go of that. Every one of us, hopefully, has chosen a delusion to work on. And we want to consider: how are we personally bringing in faith into that? What role is faith playing in our destruction of that delusion, or at least reduction of it? Are we bringing in the tool of faith?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: As we know, faith precedes all virtues. If a virtue is going to be in our mind, there needs to be faith first. Faith precedes all virtues — it's always present first before any other virtue arises. So when we're trying to understand and oppose a delusion and develop its opposite, some kind of opponent, we want to bring in faith in some way. Often the issue with working on any state of mind is that we just don't have a sufficient wish to abandon the delusion. We have a little bit of a wish, but not a wish that's bigger than our wish to do other things. And a wish that's not bigger than our wish to do other things is utterly inert. It has a karmic effect, which is nice, but has no effect to enact real change right now.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: So with any delusion, if we're not seeing some obvious movement on it, the first culprit is really to look at: what does my wish, my wishing faith, look like? Which is the wish to abandon that delusion, or wish to be free of it. What does that really look like? We can think of it as 0 to 100. Zero is, I have absolutely no interest at all. We all want it to some degree — we chose it. So it's above zero. But it's helpful to assume it's like a five. A five out of 100. The wishing faith can go way higher. For example, if it's pervading our mind in everything we do, that's getting into the 80s and 90s. It's pervading every thought we have. We're thinking, I want to be free of this delusion, it's a poison, it's only serving to harm me, I'll do anything to get rid of it. That kind of conviction — that's somewhere in the 80s and 90s. Every moment, pervading our consciousness. Lower than that, somewhere in the 40s, we have this feeling like it's still basically the most important or interesting thing in our life. We're just not always thinking about it all day. It's so clearly vital because it's part of our enlightenment.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: It's helpful to think about other things in our life that would be akin to a 40 or 50. Like sleeping. Getting enough sleep at night — that's somewhere probably around there. We're not thinking about it all day, hopefully. But it feels really important. Even the important things in my life, like going to work and making money, being friends with people, even family commitments — I still put them on hold temporarily for getting enough sleep. That's probably a 40 or 50. A strong urge, a non-negotiable intention, but not pervading our mind. Things like not obviously dying — that's somewhere in the 80s and 90s. If there was something incredibly dangerous, even if there was a huge price on it, for a lot of people we wouldn't do it because we value our life. There's that story of the dude who chopped his own arm off, stuck under a boulder, for survival. That survival mechanism is a really powerful wish. The reason we're talking about this is because often what happens is that we have a tiny little wish — and we can substitute that for being what Buddha's really talking about, wishing faith, which is like a powerful driving force where this is a priority, this is what I think about all day. Often when we're trying to make any personal change in spiritual practice, we're trying to make it with like a 2 out of 100. A very weak wish that doesn't last, runs out of steam very quickly, gets discouraged, gets replaced by a million other wishes. Then we end up going, it's not working, the practice isn't working. But we didn't actually want it that badly. We had a tiny semi-interest. It wasn't as strong as our wish for survival. But actually, getting rid of the delusions is even more important than survival. Because if you get rid of your delusions but die, you go to the pure land and benefit all living beings forever. If you stay alive but keep delusions and non-virtue going, it's almost worse. If you run the math, it really is. So it's even more important than survival.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: So how can I up my faith, my wishing faith, in overcoming this delusion? Generally, it depends on admiring and believing faith. Believing faith is sort of like: it's possible, the freedom from the delusion exists. That was the imagination practice we were doing — trying to get a mental image of what it looks like and really seeing that it is possible for us. And admiring faith is appreciating the benefits of doing so and the faults of not doing so. Really admiring the freedom from that delusion. And then from those two activities, a wishing faith will arise like a beautiful flower from the earth of the other faiths. So that's just an invitation for all of us. This section is about cultivating faith in bodhichitta by thinking of some of its good qualities. We could do this with all of our virtues that we want to work on. So that's faith as a tool for habit change.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Then, eliminating the two obstructions. 'As mentioned earlier, there are two sets of obstructions affecting the mind: obstructions to liberation and obstructions to omniscience. Bodhichitta has the power to eliminate both of these. It is like the moon, dispelling the unbearable suffering of sentient beings caused by their delusions — and in this way, it eliminates the obstructions to liberation. Furthermore, it is like the sun, dispelling the darkness of the imprints of ignorance, thereby removing the obstructions to omniscience. If we develop the precious bodhichitta and cultivate the two wings of method and wisdom, we'll be able to fly over all obstacles and reach the supreme citadel of enlightenment. Bodhichitta is like the hand holding the axe of wisdom.' Yeah! Take that! 'And by wielding the realization of emptiness, we can cut through the root of self-grasping's imprints and attain complete omniscience. In summary, when the milk of Dharma is churned by wisdom, the quintessential butter we receive is the precious bodhichitta.' But you're allowed to call it Butterchitta, if you'd like. For now. Just for today. And then you can never say it again. But we all have a pass for the next hour to call it Butterchitta. Yum-yum.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: So we've alluded to some of these points already about the importance of bodhichitta. But it's nice here to key in on this sort of obstruction. We can ask ourselves right now: what are my obstructions in my practice? Or, a better way to say it: what am I deeming an obstruction? What am I deeming an obstacle in my practice? And when we identify them, it's nice to think: why? What's the evidence that proves that it's getting in the way of our development of bodhichitta or overcoming our delusion of choice? What's the proof? Generally, the inner obstructions are the real obstructions. And those are just two types: delusions and the imprints of delusions. Those are obstructions to liberation and obstructions to omniscience. Those are the only two inner ones. And those are the real obstructions — they actually do get in the way of our path. We can say for a fact they are obstructions. Definitively. The outer ones, quote unquote — it's a lot more nebulous. What makes something an outer obstruction, precisely? Can someone come up with a clear, definitive outer obstruction? Yeah, David.

teaching.speaker: David
teaching.text: The best definition I can think of is something that's beyond our current capacity to fold into the path.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, something that's beyond our current capacity to fold into the path. I think that's a fair way to think about it. But can we come up with an example? What would be one that would say, this is an outer obstruction?

teaching.speaker: David
teaching.text: Like if you had just horrible nerve pain that pervaded your consciousness all the time, and you didn't have enough space to practice.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: But what about the person who is taking and giving with that? And uses that to motivate their taking and giving?

teaching.speaker: David
teaching.text: For that person, it's not...

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: So you're saying, if the condition was such that they had no ability to practice with it at their current level. Yeah, I think that's a decent working definition. Adriana, you have a hand there?

teaching.speaker: Adriana
teaching.text: What about the freedoms and endowments? Aren't they the definition of the human and non-human obstacles?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, I think that's a very good idea. Some of them, right now, we don't have to worry about, but we might have to worry about in future lives. Like being born in a place where Buddha has not taught, and not having Sangha, not having support from benefactors. Some of those we're good on right now. But being an animal — that's definitely an outer obstacle. Just the animal form itself is an obstacle. Being a hungry ghost, a hell being — those are clear outer obstacles. Obviously there are still delusions, but these are outer conditions that make it very hard to practice with. Some physical impairments can be — they don't have to be, but they can be. And some mental impairments can be, but again, they don't have to be. But yeah, definitely, those are nice ones to key in on as examples. Without these freedoms and endowments, the preciousness of our life starts to fall away.

teaching.speaker: Alexis
teaching.text: Maybe someone who's in a very abusive relationship, or someone who has difficulty financially in terms of living in a house and getting food. Like, that's where their constant energy goes — that survival is their priority.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, I think some of these things can be like that. Again, it has to have the rider that David noted — that they are not able to transform them. Because there are many mendicants, for example, people who just live out in the wild in Buddhist history, who are these incredible practitioners. So that on its own doesn't preclude spiritual attainments. But yeah, for some people, maybe their mental capacity would not be such that they were able to live a life like that. And so for that person, it might function like an obstacle.

teaching.speaker: Alexis
teaching.text: I was just wondering, who's deciding if it's difficult? Because maybe I think, oh my gosh, this is so beyond me. But it's still going on. And is it the Buddhas that are like, no, no, you're good, you can handle this. Who's actually deciding? When it's beyond our capacity, where does that come from?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: That's just an imputation. It's just a name that we're using. There's nothing from its own side that is permanently an outer obstacle. It's really the imputation. We're going to get to this point in a second. But viewing things as an obstacle — we have to take a huge amount of responsibility for that. A hundred percent of the responsibility for the view that something is an obstacle. We have to understand the predictive effect of viewing something as an obstacle. That's the biggest determination — that it functions like an obstacle. It's like, 'This is an obstacle.' Now it's an obstacle. It's the view, it's imputed. It's created by mind. That's the main thing that makes something an obstacle.

teaching.speaker: Anne
teaching.text: This is kind of the flip side of what David and Alexis were talking about. Incredible good worldly fortune could be a huge obstacle if you all of a sudden got very rich or successful or famous. You could just — whoop — 'I'm good.'

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, for sure. Generally speaking, it's more of an obstacle. Because there's just no interest to practice. A lot of people will pray in the trenches with the bullets flying over their head. But they won't pray getting massaged in a pleasure garden. They're not praying at that point. They're just thinking, 'I did it, I made it, it's all me.' And Geshe does explicitly list this — the sort of windfall, like getting a bunch of cash — it could very easily function like an obstacle for our practice.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: So the point of this analysis is for us to think about it for a bit. But we also want to look at our particular mind. Our mind that is particular. A better way to say it: how particular am I? How particular am I? 'I like it this way, but not that way.' It's the opposite of a bodhisattva's mind. A bodhisattva's mind is just totally open and flexible. It's just thinking about emptiness and benefiting people. It's not that different being here or there, doing this or that. They understand it's all coming from the mind anyway. So we don't need to be so particular about doing this and doing that and going here and going there. It's often a helpful test to see where we're at. Just ask yourself: how particular am I?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: That particularity has really created this idea of the world full of all these obstacles. It's kind of created this landmine universe. And that narrow path that we're trying to live on — just our particular path — we sort of juxtapose it to the rest of the world, which in our mind is like, those are all the obstacles, all the things in my way. I have to avoid them and control everything just so I can follow this exact, specific route every day. And that mind is very tight. It's fearful. There's a very close connection between being particular and being fearful. It's an anxious or fearful mind that wants to control. It can't handle uncertainty and change and variety and variability, volatility. And what happens is it's just going to really box us in. So there's a nice way to work on it: specifically looking at the attachment to things being a certain way. It's a meta type of attachment — I just want things to be a certain way. My way. And then there's various ways it manifests: I want to be here and not there, I want this kind of food and not that kind, I want to hang out with this kind of person and not that kind. All these preferences and discriminations that are very hard and fast. But all that is because we're attached to those things. We think we need them to be happy. We need those conditions to be happy. That's the very definition of attachment — looking for happiness outside of ourselves, in particular situations and conditions.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: The first step is just playing around with this thought throughout the day: I don't need it to be this way or that way. All I need to do is transform my mind. I don't need things to be this way or that way. What I really need to do is transform my mind and oppose my delusions — my real obstacles. It's just a really lovely mantra we can start to use throughout the day. We'll notice this relaxing calm that will set in, this kind of anxiety that will melt off of us when we start using this mantra. It doesn't mean we don't have a preference, but we haven't tied our happiness to being dependent on the preference. My happiness is independent of the preference. I still can have a preference, but my happiness isn't linked to it anymore. I don't need it to be this way or that way. What I really need to do is to transform my mind, to train my mind.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Then as we go through the day and encounter something that we weren't that jazzed by, we really want a blessing to not see it as an obstacle. It's not an obstacle from its own side, but it can be if we impute it that way. What we're asking for is a blessing, not for it to go away. We're asking for a blessing to not see it as an obstacle — which basically means to see it as part of our path. This is especially Dorje Shugden's function. He blesses our mind to see every condition as favorable for our practice. We can impute 'favorable' as the label. It's nice to ask for a blessing to see it that way — bless me, Dorje Shugden, Buddha, to help me see it, to impute it, to appear it as a favorable condition, as part of my path, my journey. The more we do the first part right, the less we have to do this.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Inevitably, life and our karma are going to throw something that was not in our plan. It was like, 'Fine, going to work today, I'm okay if it goes well and everyone likes me. I'm okay if everyone's in a bad mood.' We're like, 'Bring it on, I'm a bodhisattva, I'm open for anything.' We go there and we get a kidney stone. We're feeling agonizing pain. That wasn't in our plan. We were ready for anything at work, but we weren't thinking about kidney stones as one of the possibilities. Even though it was definitely in the pie chart of possibilities, we just didn't know it was. Then that gets thrown at us and we weren't ready, and we're thrown off guard. Okay, Dorje Shugden, please bless me to really not see this as an obstacle. Please bless me to see this as a favorable condition. We're asking for a spiritual guide to really bless our heart for that seeing.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Basically, we all know the teachings on transforming adversity. But we can ask ourselves: how often, when adversity strikes, do I think 'good'? How often do we go, 'Good!' Versus how often do we try to control it and resist it and change it? The adversity in our life is really helping us become more flexible. It's also helping us see the faults in being so rigid mentally, needing it one way or the other. I read about — I forget what it's called, maybe Netflix or one of these companies has, they call some of their engineers 'chaos engineers.' Chaos monkeys, chaos engineers. Basically, instead of building a perfect system and just waiting to adjust it if a bug comes up, they have random problems that someone creates for the system. Random servers shut down all throughout the country. No one knows when it's going to happen, and it just shuts down. Then it tests the system to see how adaptable it is to that kind of point of failure. It's a clever idea. It's basically saying, 'I want to be a lojong practitioner' — in a business sense. The chaos of our life is very useful. It's really helping us see things we wouldn't have seen otherwise. Actually, the more that comes now, as long as we're open to learning and training on it, the faster we're going to grow. If we keep coping and controlling everything to avoid any volatility, we might not train particularly.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: In summary, we're talking about obstructions. Technically, there's only two types: the delusional obstructions and the obstructions to omniscience. There are outer conditions — I think that point that David made, that definition, is a useful one. A condition that we are not currently able to transform into the path for some reason. There are no inherent obstacles on the outside. None of them are inherently obstacles. It's just a matter of how we see them. We need to ask for wisdom blessings. It's a type of wisdom — like an emptiness meditation. We need to ask for wisdom blessings to see these conditions as part of our journey. Does anyone have any specific questions about that? Alexis, yeah.

teaching.speaker: Alexis
teaching.text: Is what you're saying — first of all, I love what you were saying about how our job is to transform our mind, it could go this way or that way, our job is to transform our mind. Also, what you said about asking for wisdom blessings when we are seeing something as an obstacle — to please help. Would that be the hook that was mentioned before, in terms of the Buddhas can help us but we need to do our part? Is that our part?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah, thanks, Alexis. Good point. Linking it to that amazing analogy — which I did accidentally skip over — it's a very useful analogy about dependent relationship. It's like the ring and the hook. I always forget which is which. The ring is the faith and the hook is the blessings. The Buddhas want to help us and bless our mind. Not necessarily just to make things go away — unless there is no way we could ever see it as favorable. But they mostly just want to bless our mind to help us train with whatever appears. By asking for that help, making requests and offerings, asking for blessings to see our conditions as favorable — that's the faith bit. Then the blessings will come. It's a different prayer than 'make it go away.' Technically, I guess it goes away because we see it differently. But 'take it away from me so I don't have to change my view' isn't exactly what we're praying for. We're praying to have wisdom, to see it differently, and in that way dispel the obstacle. I think that's all right for now. Oh, David, yeah.

teaching.speaker: David
teaching.text: I sometimes say Tara mantras when I want things to work out. Is that a really bad habit?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Depends on what we want to work out. It's like, 'I'm going to put $10,000 on red. I'm talking to Tara, Tara's so hot.' That's clearly awful and corrupt. We're not doing that. Versus, okay, someone is really sick and I'm wishing healing for them. 'May Tara bless their mind and help them see this as meaningful and make this a spiritually meaningful experience.' That's very pure and beautiful, and so clearly compassionate. Those are two sides of the spectrum, and we have to figure out where we're at with our different requests. Ten thousand dollars on red at a roulette game is so clearly non-virtuous. Praying for someone who's sick to have spiritual wisdom and get the help they need — that's so clearly positive and virtuous. Maybe some of the things we're praying for are somewhere in between, and we've got to figure out mostly what the intention is. Sumit, thanks. Then we'll have time to discuss.

teaching.speaker: Sumit
teaching.text: I like what you're saying about, let me get a blessing to see this as beneficial. I totally get how that applies to things that have occurred — you lost your job, you got fired. My question is, you don't have to think that way for things that have not yet occurred. You could be like, A is better than B, I want the Dharma center to flourish. Is that fair to say?

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: You're asking, could we then have a wish to have a preference and to prefer one option over the other?

teaching.speaker: Sumit
teaching.text: I'm asking that because of your point about not being too particular. It's kind of like, I strongly wish for the Dharma center to flourish. That's a strong wish I have. That's how the question is coming out of it.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Yeah. Having a preference isn't the problem. It's the attachment to the preference. That's the key thing. For me, the things I have very strong preferences about, even if they're Dharma-adjacent or clearly related, it is very easy for them to be corrupted a little bit by some attachment. There's a pure wish in there and also an attached wish. It's a little bit mixed. Of course, having the wish for Dharma to flourish coming from our compassion and love — that's not attachment. That's just our bodhichitta, basically. We don't want to get rid of that. That mind, though, isn't particular. It's not obsessive and attached to 'one way or the highway.' It has this broad, open mind. It's probably thinking about Dharma flourishing over millions of lifetimes. It understands the value of karma, creating connections. It's very patient and very loving and very relaxed. It's also driven, but not in an attached way. In summary, preferences are no problem. It's just when we're attached to our preferences that's where we get into an issue. It is definitely possible for it to be with respect to our Dharma activities. Does that answer your question?

teaching.speaker: Sumit
teaching.text: You're right about the example. I guess it's more a question of my own to self-examine. There are often times where I am more particular. I want this class to go well. It's a very real lived experience where I'm like, I want this analogy to land, I want this Dharma advice to help this person. It's not over lifetimes. But I also think it's virtuous, while acknowledging that it is quite particular.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: I know it's really worth it to look at those instances, both as a teacher and as a friend to people, as a family member. That can manifest, for example, when someone is sick. We really do wish them to not be sick anymore. That can be a very virtuous wish. It can also be a very attached wish. It makes all the sense in the world on the outside — 'I want you to be healed.' But is that thought peaceful or unpeaceful? If it's unpeaceful, it's coming from attachment. If it's a peaceful thought, it's coming from our compassion. It's worth us all looking at this. It's not easy, actually. It's not easy to get it right when it's things that really align with our spiritual values. It's easier with things that are clearly vices — 'That's clearly a vice, I'm attached, I'm working on it, it's obviously a mess.' But when it's something related to our spiritual practice — these are things we view as a cause of our happiness. What's the difference between attachment and faith then? Faith in the spiritual practice versus attachment to the spiritual practice — they can look very similar. The outer behavior of someone who has a lot of faith versus someone who's attached to the idea of their practice can even look very similar. They're both feeling, 'This is a cause of my happiness.' But one of the keys is that it's a contaminated object when it's an object of attachment — viewing it as inherently existent. Part of it is also motivation, the 'why.' Minds like bodhichitta prevent the attachment from arising. But without that, the egocentric mind can hijack it and make it more of an attached purpose.

teaching.speaker: Kadam Kyle
teaching.text: Okay, so we're not going to get a final answer here right now, other than it's a really juicy and beneficial thing to think about and to ponder. I think there will be layers of surprises that are really meaningful and relaxing and comfortable that we'll get from thinking about this kind of thing. What does it mean to be attached to the idea of some spiritual aim versus just having faith in it or wishing for it? What's exactly the dividing line there? And where can we move it forward in a helpful direction? Okay, I think that's good for now. Let's have some time for discussion.

practiceDiscussion.speaker: Kadam Kyle
practiceDiscussion.text: Yeah, that's a great one too. That's nice. So good job, everyone. That's good. Both options are good applications of this technique. So this one, the nimku meditation — the purpose would be to strengthen our bodhisattva vow and resolve. The object is the feeling of happiness and rejoicing at having taken the bodhisattva vows. Thank you. We all passed the test. I'm very happy about that. Hopefully we can think about this in the future weeks. I'll keep trying to remind us every week to do this little exercise. And if we're teaching Dharma, please consider it when you're teaching and preparing your classes — okay, how am I going to actually divide the meditation into these three bits and then guide it? What I've found is the discipline makes the class way better. Regardless of what I come up with as the answer, just the discipline of trying to do that exercise makes the class way better. And sometimes I come up with the answer and I have no idea. And then I'm like, why was I going to teach that class? I have no idea what spiritual experience I'm trying to lead people towards.
